{"schema":"voice-draft-source/4","kind":"draft","draft":"An online age-checking law may be presented as a narrow safety measure: confirm that a visitor is old enough, then let the visitor proceed. That description sounds limited. The machinery required to make it work is not. An age gate can become identity infrastructure when the system collects, links, retains, or repeatedly validates information about ordinary people—and when access to common speech depends on that system.

The first question is what “checking age” actually requires. A service could ask for a credential, a facial image, a payment-card signal, a phone number, or a third-party assertion (each method carries a different burden). The law may say that the service need only know whether someone is above a threshold. The technical process may still create a durable record of who sought access, when, and through which device. A narrow legal label does not narrow the data path.

That path can expand quietly. A company may retain an image to resolve disputes. It may connect an age result to an account, an advertising profile, or a fraud database (even when the original purpose was limited). A vendor may offer one verification service to many websites, making a single identity signal useful across places that were never meant to share a reader. The database becomes more than an age check; it becomes a map of participation.

Supporters of an age-checking requirement can point to a legitimate aim. Children deserve protection from material designed to exploit their attention, and a carefully designed gate may reduce some access. That concession matters. It doesn't answer the central privacy problem: what happens when proving eligibility requires identification? If a person must hand over a face, document, or persistent identifier to read lawful material, the system changes the cost of participation.

The danger isn't limited to a breach. A database can be misused through ordinary legal demands, internal access, inaccurate matches, or later policy changes. Information gathered for one purpose can acquire new value when officials, companies, or investigators discover that it already exists. A system built to separate adults from children may become attractive for tracking political reading, health questions, sexuality, religion, or unpopular views (the categories most in need of privacy). That is a structural risk, not a dramatic edge case.

The law's disclaimer may insist that the system is not an identity registry. That does not settle the matter. A registry is defined by what an infrastructure can do, not only by what a statute calls it. If the same service can recognize a person across websites, preserve a history of checks, or link an age token to a name, it has acquired identity functions—even if each individual transaction is described as anonymous. The label cannot erase the capability.

We should test the proposal at the point of use, where abstractions meet a reader. What happens when you open a site about a controversial subject and a gate demands a document? Do you leave a record of that attempt? Can an error block access, and can the person correct it? Can the company sell the signal, share it with another service, or keep it after the visit? Those questions expose the infrastructure more clearly than the bill's narrow purpose.

A privacy-preserving design may improve the situation. A verifier could return a limited yes-or-no result, avoid storing raw documents, separate identity from browsing, and permit independent deletion (with deletion proved rather than merely promised). Strong limits on retention, sharing, compelled disclosure, and secondary use could reduce the danger. But we're still entitled to ask whether the system is necessary for the stated goal, and whether less identifying methods are available.

Our position is simple: safety rules should protect children without turning access to lawful information into a demand for identification. We're asking lawmakers to define data minimization, prohibit cross-site tracking, require real remedies for errors, and make independent audits public. They should also explain what happens when a vendor fails, changes ownership, or closes. If those safeguards are absent, the age check is not a small gate at the edge of the internet. An online age-checking law may be presented as a narrow safety measure: confirm that a visitor is old enough, then let the visitor proceed. That description sounds limited. The machinery required to make it work is not. An age gate can become identity infrastructure when the system collects, links, retains, or repeatedly validates information about ordinary people—and when access to common speech depends on that system.

The first question is what “checking age” actually requires. A service could ask for a credential, a facial image, a payment-card signal, a phone number, or a third-party assertion (each method carries a different burden). The law may say that the service need only know whether someone is above a threshold. The technical process may still create a durable record of who sought access, when, and through which device. A narrow legal label does not narrow the data path.

That path can expand quietly. A company may retain an image to resolve disputes. It may connect an age result to an account, an advertising profile, or a fraud database (even when the original purpose was limited). A vendor may offer one verification service to many websites, making a single identity signal useful across places that were never meant to share a reader. The database becomes more than an age check; it becomes a map of participation.

Supporters of an age-checking requirement can point to a legitimate aim. Children deserve protection from material designed to exploit their attention, and a carefully designed gate may reduce some access. That concession matters. It doesn't answer the central privacy problem: what happens when proving eligibility requires identification? If a person must hand over a face, document, or persistent identifier to read lawful material, the system changes the cost of participation.

The danger isn't limited to a breach. A database can be misused through ordinary legal demands, internal access, inaccurate matches, or later policy changes. Information gathered for one purpose can acquire new value when officials, companies, or investigators discover that it already exists. A system built to separate adults from children may become attractive for tracking political reading, health questions, sexuality, religion, or unpopular views (the categories most in need of privacy). That is a structural risk, not a dramatic edge case.

The law's disclaimer may insist that the system is not an identity registry. That does not settle the matter. A registry is defined by what an infrastructure can do, not only by what a statute calls it. If the same service can recognize a person across websites, preserve a history of checks, or link an age token to a name, it has acquired identity functions—even if each individual transaction is described as anonymous. The label cannot erase the capability.

We should test the proposal at the point of use, where abstractions meet a reader. What happens when you open a site about a controversial subject and a gate demands a document? Do you leave a record of that attempt? Can an error block access, and can the person correct it? Can the company sell the signal, share it with another service, or keep it after the visit? Those questions expose the infrastructure more clearly than the bill's narrow purpose.

A privacy-preserving design may improve the situation. A verifier could return a limited yes-or-no result, avoid storing raw documents, separate identity from browsing, and permit independent deletion (with deletion proved rather than merely promised). Strong limits on retention, sharing, compelled disclosure, and secondary use could reduce the danger. But we're still entitled to ask whether the system is necessary for the stated goal, and whether less identifying methods are available.

Our position is simple: safety rules should protect children without turning access to lawful information into a demand for identification. We're asking lawmakers to define data minimization, prohibit cross-site tracking, require real remedies for errors, and make independent audits public. They should also explain what happens when a vendor fails, changes ownership, or closes. If those safeguards are absent, the age check is not a small gate at the edge of the internet. It is a foundation poured beneath it, and the public will live with whatever gets built there.
